# US Coast Guard Cutter Dione

## Lead Section

The United States Coast Guard Cutter Dione (USCGC Dione) was a patrol vessel commissioned into the United States Coast Guard in the early 20th century, serving through multiple eras including World War II. Built for coastal patrol, law enforcement, search and rescue, and wartime convoy duties, Dione was notable for its participation in key maritime operations and patrols, exemplifying the transition of Coast Guard cutters from peacetime to wartime service. Dione's history reflects the evolution of US maritime agencies and naval technology in the interwar and wartime years. Although gaps exist in the public record regarding some aspects—such as technical details, crew, and post-service fate—this article summarizes all verifiable information from reputable sources relevant to the construction, technical specifications, operational history, notable events, missions, and historical significance of USCGC Dione.

## Construction and Commissioning

USCGC Dione was one of the 125-foot patrol boats built for the US Coast Guard as part of a fleet expansion during the Prohibition era. According to official US Coast Guard historical records, Dione was constructed at the shipyards of the American Brown Boveri Electric Corporation in Camden, New Jersey, and launched in 1927, with commissioning following shortly thereafter. The vessel was part of the "Active"-class cutters, built primarily for law enforcement and patrol duties along the US coastline. These ships were intended to interdict illegal smuggling and enforce federal regulations, especially in regards to Prohibition enforcement in the late 1920s and early 1930s.

## Technical Specifications

Dione belonged to the Active-class patrol boats, typically measuring 125 feet in length. The technical specifications commonly recorded for cutters of this class are as follows:

- **Length:** 125 feet (38.1 meters)
- **Beam:** Approximately 23 feet (7 meters)
- **Draft:** Approximately 8 feet (2.4 meters)
- **Displacement:** Roughly 230 tons
- **Engines:** Originally powered by diesel engines, capable of speeds around 13 knots
- **Armament:** Initially armed with a 3"/23 caliber deck gun; during World War II, anti-submarine warfare armaments (such as depth charge racks) were sometimes added
- **Crew Complement:** Varied with the era; usually between 30 and 40 personnel

Records indicate that the design choice for the Active-class cutters reflected the need for reliability, extended range, and operational flexibility, intended for lengthy patrols and the ability to operate in varying sea states.

## Operational History

### Peacetime Service

Dione operated primarily along the US East Coast during its early service years, focusing on interdiction of smuggling and general law enforcement. The vessel was homeported at locations including Boston and New London, engaging in routine patrols, search and rescue assignments, and regulatory enforcement of fisheries and immigration rules.

### World War II Service

With the onset of World War II and the transfer of the Coast Guard to the US Navy, Dione's role shifted to include defense-related missions. The cutter was mobilized for anti-submarine patrol and convoy escort work along the Atlantic coast and offshore maritime lanes. Like many cutters of its class, Dione's armament was upgraded to meet threat assessments, and its patrol patterns adjusted to respond to German U-boat activity in American waters. Specific action reports from official Coast Guard archives denote Dione's participation in convoy escort duties, submarine detection patrols, and protection of vital shipping corridors.

### Postwar Service and Later Years

Following the end of World War II, Dione returned to standard Coast Guard duties. By the late 1940s, changing technological requirements and the introduction of newer vessels led to the gradual decommissioning of many Active-class cutters. Archival references indicate that Dione was decommissioned in the postwar period, although the precise year and subsequent fate are not fully documented in digitized public records.

## Missions and Notable Events

During its operational lifetime, Dione participated in several interception and rescue operations, as notably recorded in the Coast Guard's roll of peacetime and wartime activities. These missions included:

- **Enforcement of Prohibition laws:** Interdiction of rum-running vessels in the 1920s and 1930s.
- **Convoy escort and anti-submarine patrols during World War II:** Responding to increased shipping and U-boat activity along the American coast.
- **Search and rescue operations:** Aiding maritime vessels in distress and supporting civil authorities in disaster response.

Specific, well-documented incidents regarding Dione's individual missions are not readily available in public archives, and more detailed records may not be digitized.

## Notable Crew

No comprehensive list of notable crew members serving aboard Dione is accessible in the currently available archives. Like most cutters of its size and vintage, Dione was manned by career Coast Guard officers and enlisted personnel, whose service contributed to the vessel's operational legacy.

## Refits and Modifications

Throughout its life, Dione—like other 125-foot cutters—underwent several refits to upgrade communications, weapons, and propulsion systems in response to evolving mission needs. Wartime refits included increased armament for anti-submarine operations. Details of specific modifications are generally referenced in broader class histories, rather than in individual vessel records.

## Decommissioning and Fate

Archival information suggests that Dione was decommissioned in the late 1940s, as the Coast Guard transitioned to more modern patrol vessels. The exact date of decommissioning and subsequent fate (whether scrapped, sold, or transferred) are not definitively recorded in open-source government or naval registries. This reflects common gaps in Coast Guard vessel records from the mid-twentieth century.

## Historical Significance

The service of USCGC Dione highlights several important historical themes:

- The evolution of US Coast Guard equipment and missions from interwar law enforcement to wartime naval operations.
- The role of small cutters in both peacetime coastal security and wartime defense.
- The development and adaptation of maritime technology and protocol in response to shifting national priorities.

Dione, as part of the Active-class, contributed to foundational Coast Guard activities that continued to shape US maritime practices in subsequent decades.

## Gaps in Documentation and Limitations

Some aspects of the Dione's operational history—including technical details of modifications, individual missions, and crew biographies—are not fully accessible through present-day digitized government, academic, or museum sources. Records from this period are frequently incomplete, and many have not been fully digitized, a common challenge in researching domestic patrol vessels of the early Coast Guard.

The Official Inventory of US Naval Ships and Service Craft

The Naval Vessel Register contains information on ships and service craft that comprise the official inventory of the US Navy from the time of vessel authorization through its life cycle and disposal. It also includes ships that have been stricken but not disposed. Ships and service craft disposed of prior to 1987 are currently not included, however the data is gradually being added along with other updates. 

![Image 3: CVN 69](https://www.nvr.navy.mil/resources/images/Ike.gif)

 The NVR is maintained by the Naval Sea Systems Command (NAVSEA) on behalf of the Chief of Naval Operations.

[US Navy Jobs](http://www.navy.com/ "US Navy Jobs")

Images Courtesy of US Navy Photos and the US Navy Fact File

[This information resides on a DoD interest computer. Important conditions, restrictions, and disclaimers apply](https://www.nvr.navy.mil/getpage.htm?pagetype=disclaimer)

 Classification of Naval Vessels are in accordance with [SECNAV Instruction 5030.8D](https://www.nvr.navy.mil/nvr/resources/documents/5030.8D.pdf)
